papers.title: Circadian rhythm in the atrioventricular node - in electrophysiology, contractility, metabolism, intracellular signalling and extracellular matrix
papers.abstract: The atrioventricular (AV) node shows a circadian rhythm-during sleep the PR interval is longer (because conduction velocity is decreased) and AV block is more common. We show the rhythm is similar in mouse and human, and using mice we have investigated the cause. There was still a rhythm in Kcnj5 knockout mice ruling out a major role of vagal tone (the vagus regulates the node via Kcnj5). Instead, we show the presence of a functioning circadian clock in the node (e.g. by detection of rhythmic clock transcripts). There was ~43-52% reduction in the rhythm of the PR interval on inhibition of the clock in a Bmal1 knockout mouse. There was a significant rhythm in >300 intracellular signalling molecules presumably driven by the clock and perhaps extrinsic signals. Downstream of the clock and signalling molecules, there was a rhythm in many transcripts and proteins (of 4,186 proteins, ~15% had a rhythm), responsible for example for contractile machinery, metabolism, extracellular matrix, and importantly ion channels. Ultimately, the PR interval is determined by ion channels, and there were rhythms in ion channels and ionic currents. A key determinant of conduction velocity is the upstroke velocity of the Ca2+-dependent nodal action potential and this was significantly reduced during sleep, this can be explained by reduced expression of Ca2+ channel subunits and a smaller L-type Ca2+ current at this time and this was confirmed by biophysically-detailed computer modelling. In conclusion, there is day-night molecular remodelling of the AV node and this is largely responsible for the circadian rhythm in the PR interval.

papers.title: Image-grounded encoding models reveal distinct temporal profiles of naturalistic object and scene processing in the human brain
papers.abstract: In real-world vision, the human brain needs to process large amounts of information to effectively interact with its environment. It is well established that our visual system has specialized regions to process information efficiently, such as scene-, face-, and object-selective areas, which can be uncovered using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). However, functional localizers typically use artificially separated stimuli (e.g. scene backgrounds vs. object cutouts), and fMRI signals are insensitive to potential temporal processing differences. Here, we identify temporal signatures of object and scene processing in real-world visual environments by building image-grounded brain-predictive encoding models of human electroencephalography (EEG) responses. In a large set of high-resolution natural images, we first separate object-bound from scene-bound features on a per-image basis, and then used these features to train separate deep neural network-based encoding models to predict EEG responses to the full, intact images. We find that encoding models trained on object-bound features consistently exhibit a delayed temporal encoding profile compared to models trained on scene-bound features. Control analyses confirm the robustness of this delayed object encoding, showing that a consistent separation of objects from scene parts is needed to achieve a temporal distinction. Using these distinct encoding profiles as processing templates, we reveal the typicality of individual image elements as objects or part of the scene. These findings demonstrate that object and scene processing in the human brain unfold differentially over time and indicate that image-grounded encoding models are helpful tools for isolating components of naturalistic visual perception.

papers.title: Pooled sequencing reveals patterns of underlying genomic divergence in Drosophila chronotypes
papers.abstract: Chronotypes, often referred to in the context of sleep timing in humans (early/late sleepers) are heritable variations in timing of circadian behaviours. Chronotype differences among individuals have been associated with a myriad of psychological, metabolic, and physiological dysregulations. Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) in humans have identified several circadian clock gene polymorphisms associated with divergent chronotypes; however, the lists of candidate genes vary across studies based on methodology and sampling strategy thus, necessitating more controlled studies on well-established model systems. Using long-term experimental evolution approach spanning over 20 years, we have derived a unique set of chronotypes in the form of 12 replicate Drosophila melanogaster populations that exhibit early/morning and late/evening emergence and have previously reported several circadian clock differences between the populations. We performed pooled DNA sequencing to explore genomic differences underlying early and late chronotypes and identified multiple genomic regions under selection. We observe that the early chronotype populations have primarily accumulated polymorphisms in genes related to photosensitivity, sleep, and the circadian clock, while the late chronotype populations have largely accumulated polymorphisms in genes related to the circadian clock, mRNA splicing mechanisms, and ecdysis. We further predict biological pathways under differential selection in the early and late chronotype populations. We believe these results provide evolutionary mechanisms behind chronotype divergence and will help generate verifiable hypothesis regarding target genes for phase divergence.

papers.title: Harnessing Circadian Resilience for Demand-Flexible Controlled Environment Agriculture
papers.abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable electricity generation creates opportunities for flexible demand-side energy management in Total Controlled Environment Agriculture (TCEA), where artificial lighting represents a major operational cost. However, the biological consequences of demand-responsive lighting strategies remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether photoperiods can be dynamically adjusted to minimise economic costs or maximise renewable energy utilisation while maintaining crop productivity. Using historical electricity market and wind-generation data, we evaluated three demand-flexing strategies: short-term demand-side response (DSR) events, cost-optimised photoperiods aligned with low electricity prices, and wind-optimised photoperiods aligned with periods of high renewable generation. Despite substantial variation in photoperiod length, plants maintained robust circadian rhythms under both cost- and wind-optimised regimes, demonstrating considerable resilience of the circadian system to irregular environmental timing. Commercial-scale trials involving basil, lettuce, mustard greens and rocket revealed that demand-flexed lighting regimes had minimal effects on harvested fresh or dry weight. Our findings demonstrate that TCEA can provide meaningful demand-side flexibility and support renewable energy integration without substantial reductions in crop productivity. Circadian resilience appears to buffer plants against fluctuating photoperiods, providing a biological foundation for the deployment of demand-flexible lighting strategies in future low-carbon agricultural systems.

papers.title: State-dependent gating of sensory and cortical inputs by median raphe neurons
papers.abstract: The mesopontine median raphe (MnR) plays an important role in regulating brain states, hippocampal network activity, and memory processes. Recent studies have revealed that the MnR comprises three major neuronal populations: serotonergic (5-HT), glutamatergic (Vglut3-expressing), and GABAergic neurons. How these distinct neuronal populations may gate sensory and cortical inputs across different brain states remains largely unknown. Here, we combined in vivo electrophysiological recording, sensory or optogenetic stimulation, and transgenic approaches to characterize the response properties of 5-HT, Vglut3, and GABAergic MnR neurons during wakefulness and sleep. We found that MnR neurons exhibited pronounced state-dependent responses to both sensory and cortical stimulation, with response amplitudes significantly greater during slow-wave sleep than during wakefulness. Auditory and somatosensory stimuli elicited fast responses in the MnR: 5-HT neurons were primarily suppressed, whereas Vglut3 and GABAergic neurons were primarily activated, suggesting the presence of direct inputs from sensory thalamic or brainstem structures. Retrograde tracing identified several brainstem structures and, notably, the medial prefrontal cortex as sources of direct projections to the MnR. Optogenetic stimulation of prefrontal inputs to the MnR evoked inhibition of 5-HT neurons but robust excitation of Vglut3 neurons during slow-wave sleep, suggesting top-down control of MnR activity by the prefrontal cortex. Together, these findings reveal that the MnR exhibits enhanced sensitivity to both ascending sensory and descending cortical inputs during sleep, suggesting that it may integrate environmental and cortical signals to regulate hippocampal network activity and gate sleep-dependent memory processing.

papers.title: Waveform morphology links local circuit kinetics to cortical interactions
papers.abstract: How does local cortical physiology shape interactions between brain regions? We combined neural mass modelling with human and macaque intracranial recordings to examine how synaptic kinetics link oscillatory waveform morphology to cortical interactions. In a modified excitatory-inhibitory Wilson-Cowan model, synaptic rise and decay kinetics shaped waveform geometry and phase-dependent responsiveness. Local kinetics and coupling symmetry jointly influenced interaction measures and temporal irreversibility, while phase-locked perturbations altered imaginary coherency and bivariate irreversibility even when the coupling strengths remained fixed. In stereo-EEG from 23 patients, waveform asymmetry was most strongly associated with local irreversibility, whereas mean instantaneous alpha frequency showed stronger associations with interregional measures. Subdural macaque electrocorticography reproduced the frequency associations but not the local waveform association. Together, these findings show that waveform shape carries information about local neuronal dynamics, provide a mechanistic framework for interpreting cortical interactions, and motivate testing waveform morphology as a guide to stimulation timing.

papers.title: MRI-Based Glymphatic Markers and Their Associations with Polysomnographic Sleep in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: The glymphatic system is the brain waste clearance pathway. Although its dysfunction has been associated with several neurological disorders, its role in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains poorly understood. Glymphatic activity is thought to peak during sleep, yet its relationship with objectively measured sleep has scarcely been explored in humans. We assessed two MRI glymphatic proxies in patients with relapsing-remitting MS (PwMS) and healthy controls (HCs) and their associations with polysomnographic measures, structural MRI, and, in PwMS, disease burden. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, PwMS (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] [≤]4.0) and matched HCs underwent overnight polysomnography and 3T MRI. Glymphatic proxies were the diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and coupling of the global blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal with CSF inflow (gBOLD-CSF coupling). We also assessed sleep micro- and macroarchitecture, EDSS, disease duration, lesion volume, mean diffusivity (MD), lateral ventricle (LV) and choroid plexus volumes. Analyses were adjusted for age and sex. Results: We included 22 PwMS (34.2{+/-}10.1 years; 16 female) and 26 HCs (32.2{+/-}5.7 years; 18 female). DTI-ALPS was lower in PwMS (adjusted difference: -0.12, 95% CI -0.22 to -0.02), but MD was higher, and adjustment for MD attenuated this difference (-0.11, -0.21 to -0.0002). gBOLD-CSF coupling did not differ between groups (-0.02, -0.08 to 0.05). In PwMS, stronger coupling was associated with shorter total sleep time (r=0.49, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.77) and higher arousal index (r=-0.48, -0.77 to -0.04), whereas DTI-ALPS was unrelated to sleep. Associations with clinical and structural measures were borderline for DTI-ALPS and EDSS (r=-0.44, -0.74 to 0.01) and for coupling and LV volume (r=0.44, -0.00 to 0.74), and weak otherwise. Analyses were exploratory and uncorrected for multiplicity. Discussion: In MS, the DTI-ALPS index is partly confounded by white matter damage and should not serve as a standalone glymphatic marker. Stronger gBOLD-CSF coupling was associated with shorter, fragmented sleep in PwMS, consistent with the proposed compensatory waking CSF dynamics. If confirmed longitudinally, gBOLD-CSF coupling may serve as a glymphatic-related marker in MS and sleep a potential target to improve brain clearance in PwMS.

papers.title: Successful retrieval is its own reward
papers.abstract: The ability to successfully remember past events is critical to our daily lives, yet the neural mechanisms underlying the motivation to retrieve is unclear. Although reward-system activity and feedback-related signals have been observed during memory retrieval, whether this signal reflects intrinsic reward or goal-attainment is unknown. Adjudicating between these two alternatives is crucial for understanding how individuals are motivated to engage in retrieval and how retrieval supports later remembering. To test these two accounts, we conducted between-subjects recognition memory tasks on human participants undergoing scalp electroencephalography and varied test-phase goals (recognize old vs. detect new items). We used an independently validated feedback classifier to measure positive feedback evidence. We find positive feedback following successful retrieval regardless of task goals. Together, these results suggest that successful retrieval is intrinsically rewarding. Such a feedback signal may promote future retrieval attempts as well as bolster later memory for the successfully retrieved events.

papers.title: A Latent Variable Perspective on EEG Measures of Attentional Control
papers.abstract: Attentional control is a core cognitive function, yet there is still a significant debate revolving around its definition, factorial structure and underlying neural mechanisms. Research in this domain has largely developed along two largely disconnected traditions. Psychometric approaches assess individual differences using latent-variable models (e.g., structural equation modeling, confirmatory factor analysis), while cognitive neuroscience focuses on group-level behavioral and neural effects. This raises a critical question: can neural measures robust at the group level validly capture stable individual differences? Or more specifically, can some of the principles and analytical methods adopted in individual-differences research be directly applied to neural correlates of attentional control? The current study aims to address this question. Electroencephalogram data were recorded from participants as they completed four attentional control paradigms: a change detection task, the go/no-go task, the Simon task, and the Stroop task. From each task, we extracted the P3 component and a data-driven decoding accuracy measure as indices of conflict processing and tested whether these neural measures load onto a common latent factor of attentional control. Results revealed weak and largely non-significant correlations. Structural-equation modeling provided no evidence for a common latent factor, despite robust within-task effects at the group level reflected both in the behavioral and the EEG parameters. These findings suggest that EEG components may lack the construct validity needed to reliably capture individual differences in attentional control.

papers.title: Electrophysiological dynamics of empathy for self- and other-related pain
papers.abstract: Empathy requires the ability to generate shared representations of the self and others while maintaining a distinction between them. However, it remains unclear whether, and to what extent, the neural processes involved in sharing and understanding others' pain overlap with those involved in processing one's own pain, particularly with respect to their temporal dynamics. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying empathic processing of self- and other-related painful facial expressions. To this end, EEG signals were recorded from 42 female participants while they viewed self- and other-related painful and neutral expressions. During the early stage of processing, the difference in N2 amplitude between self-related and other-related stimuli was smaller in the painful than in the neutral condition. Nevertheless, self-related painful stimuli continued to elicit more negative N2 amplitudes and greater Alpha/Mu suppression than other-related painful stimuli. In contrast, during the late stage of empathic processing, no distinction was observed between self- and other-related painful stimuli. Instead, painful expressions, regardless of whether they were self- or other-related, elicited larger late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes. These findings suggest that empathic processing is characterized by an early self-other distinction followed by a later convergence in the neural representation of self- and other-related pain.

papers.title: Label-Free Lymphocyte Subtype and State Classification by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
papers.abstract: Accurate immune cell subtype and functional state profiling are essential for studying immune regulation, disease progression, and therapeutic response. Established single-cell analysis techniques rely heavily on either endpoint, destructive measurements or complex labeling that can potentially affect cell functions. Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy offers quantitative, label-free imaging of cells and tissues by providing contrast based on subcellular concentrations of intrinsic biomolecules at high spatial and temporal resolution. Here, we demonstrate that Vision Transformer based hyperspectral SRS imaging classification can accurately and non-destructively classify various lymphocyte phenotypes, including lymphocyte lineage (T and B cells), T cell subset and differentiation state (CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, effector, memory, and naive for both), and functional states (naive T, activated T, exhausted T) using fluorescent markers for training. By leveraging attention-based spatial-spectral feature learning, the approach captures biomolecular patterns associated with immune cell identity and state while preserving cells for downstream or longitudinal analysis. This provides a potential platform for label-free immune profiling, live-cell analysis, and longitudinal studies of immune cell type and state transitions.

papers.title: Multisensory brain processing is associated with depressive symptoms in youth with chronic pain
papers.abstract: Juvenile fibromyalgia (JFM) is a chronic pain condition marked by widespread musculoskeletal pain and often accompanied by physical fatigue, nonrestorative sleep, headaches, anxiety, and depression. Previous studies have found that adolescents with fibromyalgia report augmented unpleasantness and altered brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimuli. Likewise, research in major depression has shown altered neural processing of sensory stimulation. We examined whether augmented brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimulation is associated with depressive symptoms in adolescent girls with JFM. Forty-six female adolescents with JFM (mean - SD, 16.43 - 1.10 years [range 13-18 years]) and 44 healthy participants (mean - SD, 16.09 - 1.06 years [range 13-18 years]) completed validated questionnaires assessing daily-life sensory hypersensitivity and depressive symptoms, alongside undergoing a functional MRI multisensory task. JFM patients reported significantly higher sensory unpleasantness than healthy participants, and this hypersensitivity was positively associated with depressive symptoms. Neuroimaging results in chronic pain patients revealed that greater depressive symptomatology was associated with increased activation in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) (pFWE<0.05), a region implicated in self-referential processing and specifically rumination in adults with chronic pain. JFM patients showed increased PCC-left middle temporal gyrus task-dependent connectivity using psychophysiological interactions analysis (PPI). Furthermore, hyperconnectivity between the PCC and brain areas involved in cognitive-affective regulation, sensory integration, and memory processing was strongly correlated with depressive symptoms in JFM patients. These findings underscore the role of depressive symptoms in sensory processing and integration in JFM patients and highlight the complex interplay between sensory processing and emotional/self-referential brain function in patients.
